# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

response:
## Overall assessment

Sections 1–5 are a valuable re-analysis. The authors found real problems in the Halden pilot using its own microdata:

- Organisations dropped out after the schedule had started.
- Managers' reported output was higher than their organisations' records showed.
- Actual hours fell by less than scheduled hours.
- The revenue figure was not adjusted for inflation.

Several of these confirm points I raised about the Halden paper, with harder evidence. The conclusion does not follow from the analysis, though. Their own best estimate is a +10.8% per-hour gain, and the step from there to "entirely an artifact" rests on an extrapolated survey trend. It also ignores the randomised evidence the authors themselves call the most reliable.

## Arithmetic checks

**These pass:**
- Table 2: 95.1/0.8 gives +18.9%, 98.4/0.859 gives +14.6%, and 95.4/0.861 gives +10.8%.
- Hours: 40.3 → 34.6 is −14.1%, and 40.4 → 34.8 is −13.9%.
- Real revenue: 1.014/1.041 = 0.974, or −2.6%.

**Two do not:**

1. **The hours breakdown doesn't add up to the total.** The paper explains the gap between scheduled and actual hours as four longer days (+0.7 h each) plus 1.6 h logged on the day off. Applied to the schedule:
   - From 32 scheduled hours: 32 + 2.8 + 1.6 = 36.4 h.
   - From the baseline day length of 8.06 h: 4 × 8.76 + 1.6 ≈ 36.6 h.

   Both are about 2 hours above the reported 34.6 h. Either the components or the total is wrong. If the components are right, actual hours fell by only ~9.5%, and the corrected per-hour gain is smaller still. The authors should reconcile the two figures.

2. **The novelty extrapolation date is wrong.** Energy fell from 0.61 to 0.29 SD between months 3 and 6, about 0.107 SD per month. Continuing that line reaches zero at about month 8.7, not "around month ten". This is minor, but see point 4 below on whether the extrapolation is meaningful at all.

Also, in Section 1, six exit forms cite workload and two cite scheduling. That accounts for eight of the nine withdrawals. What did the ninth give?

## Main problems

**1. "Entirely an artifact" goes beyond the evidence.**
After the corrections the paper actually performs, a 10.8% gain remains. The jump from there to zero rests on Section 6, and it also widens the claim from one pilot to "reduced-hours schemes" in general. The Data note correctly says the corrected estimates describe only the subsets, not even the whole Halden pilot. The Abstract and Conclusion don't respect that caveat.

**2. Attrition is listed as corrected, but it isn't.**
The Abstract says "correcting the first three" problems, and the first is attrition. Table 2 adjusts only the output measure and the hours denominator. The Conclusion then counts attrition among the problems that together explain the gain.

The attrition finding is important. Halden's account ("withdrew during the preparation phase") appears to be wrong. But its effect on the estimate is never quantified. Some options:
- Bounding analysis under worst-case assumptions for the nine withdrawn organisations.
- Lee bounds.
- At minimum, a stated assumption about what output those organisations would have had.

Without one of these, attrition shows the estimate is biased upward but not by how much. A related point: the abstract says four problems "account for most of the reported gain", yet revenue never enters the per-hour calculation.

**3. The record-based index is treated as the true value without justification.**
It is more objective than managers' ratings, but it has its own problems. For example, "billable hours delivered" in professional services partly measures hours worked, so it will fall when hours are cut, whatever happens to productivity. Counts of tickets or cases ignore changes in complexity or quality.

The 23 organisations that submitted records also selected themselves. The authors should also say whether their means are employee-weighted, as Halden's were, or simple averages across organisations.

**4. The novelty argument is weak.**
- **Two data points.** The trend is fitted to two survey waves, and the first wave comes after an initial rise. That is not enough to establish a linear decline.
- **Energy isn't output.** Self-reported energy is not productivity. If novelty drove the gain, the microdata should show output per hour declining from month to month. Halden collected the output index monthly, so this can be tested directly. If per-hour output held steady from month 3 to month 6 while energy fell, that is evidence *against* the novelty account.
- **Burden of proof.** "The burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter" is a position, not a finding. With six months of data, the honest conclusion is that durability is unknown.

**5. The comment uses the Varden trial selectively.**
It calls Varden's counter stratum "the most reliable finding in the literature". But that same randomised trial reports:
- **Case-processing:** +12.5% per actual hour (CI +6.9 to +18.4).
- **Counter stratum:** +6.7% per actual hour.

That trial had a control group, administrative output records, timesheet hours and nine months of follow-up, which addresses most of the comment's concerns. It is the strongest evidence available against the "entirely an artifact" claim, and the comment doesn't engage with it. Varden has its own limitations: few offices, possibly over-narrow confidence intervals, and unlogged hours. But the comment needs to argue against it, not omit it.

**6. Section 7 misdescribes the Varden meetings analysis and applies a double standard.**
- **The offices weren't selected.** The seven offices are all the treated case-processing offices, not a subgroup picked after the results were known.
- **Varden already gave these caveats.** Its authors said it was unregistered, said it "cannot establish a mechanism", and registered a confirmatory test.
- **The same standard should apply to Section 6.** The comment's own novelty explanation is a post hoc account of a two-point survey trend. It deserves the scepticism Section 7 applies to Varden.

A fair version of Section 7 would agree the meetings link is unconfirmed. It could add the substantive weakness I noted in the Varden paper: meeting time was measured only at month six, so no office's *cut* in meetings was actually observed.

**7. No uncertainty is reported.**
Every corrected estimate comes from 17–27 organisations, and none has a confidence interval. The 11.2% retail figure rests on three organisations.

## Smaller points

- **Retail.** Section 5 could cite Halden's own reversion data, which supports its point: 3 of 6 retail and hospitality organisations reverted, against none of the 50 in the four office-based sectors.
- **CPI as a deflator.** Consumer prices are only a rough deflator for firm revenue, because sector output prices may have moved differently. The direction of the correction is right, though.
- **Unlogged work.** "Some further work on the day off is probably not logged" is plausible but unsupported. Flag it as speculation, or point to evidence.
- **Recommendations.** The list is sound and matches the Varden design, apart from the 18-month minimum.

## What the evidence supports

A defensible conclusion would read roughly as follows:

> Correcting for actual hours and record-based output, in the subsets where this is possible, reduces the Halden pilot's per-hour gain from 23.4% to about 11%. Non-random attrition likely biases this further upward by an unknown amount, and six months cannot establish durability. Combined with randomised evidence from Varden County, the best-supported picture is a moderate per-hour gain in work not tied to presence, and a net output loss where output depends on presence.

That is a strong and useful comment. The current version weakens it by claiming more than the corrections show.

## How the three papers fit together

- **Halden overstated its result,** through scheduled hours, manager ratings and survivors.
- **Varden** is the most credible of the three, though its small number of offices limits precision.
- **This comment** correctly deflates Halden but then overcorrects.

The three agree on the two points that seem most secure. Gains per scheduled hour overstate the real effect substantially. And where output depends on staff being present, reduced hours cost output.

I can draft a reply to the comment or a reviewer report if that would help.
